conditions: open with the least access that works -- PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION plus PROCESS_VM_READ; never PROCESS_VM_WRITE or PROCESS_VM_OPERATION

level_1_external_read_only_inspector.description: a separate process that opens the game process with read-only access and never writes, never injects, never hooks
reasoning: no anti-cheat middleware, no kernel driver and no service registration was found on any tested surface, so there is no known component that could observe another process opening a handle
an external reader does not modify the target, does not load a module into it and does not patch it, so the shapes that a protection layer normally reacts to are absent by construction
the residual risk is NOT protection but ordinary process hygiene: a read of a moving structure can tear, and a handle with more access than needed is a self-inflicted hazard
residual_unknowns: whether the process reacts to a foreign handle at all is not readable from the image; it becomes observable the first time level 1 is used, and the first run should therefore be treated as an experiment with a recorded expectation
level_1_external_read_only_inspector.why: both questions came back NOT FOUND WITHIN TESTED SURFACE with every control probe passing

level_2_in_process_probe.description: code running inside the game process; requires the documented escalation of plan.md section 8.4
preconditions_before_reconsidering: the two TLS callbacks of MISERY-Win64-Shipping.exe disassembled and shown to be the MSVC CRT pair, or shown not to be
a call-graph pass showing that no probe API result reaches a branch that changes behaviour
a concrete research question that level 1 provably cannot answer -- plan.md section 8.4 criterion, not a convenience
the level-1 first-contact experiment already run and recorded without incident
reasoning: this pass answers 'nothing found on the tested surfaces', not 'nothing is there'. The two questions that matter most for an in-process probe -- what the TLS callbacks do, and whether any probe API result reaches a branch -- are exactly the two this tool cannot read
an in-process probe changes the module list, allocates executable memory and may patch code. Those are the shapes a protection layer reacts to, so the margin for error is much smaller than at level 1
plan.md section 8.6 already makes level 1 the default and level 2 an escalation with a written justification; nothing here removes that requirement

census.limits: only the first 16 bytes of each callback are compared, and two functions can agree there and diverge later. This bounds the unknown, it does not close it. Closing it means disassembling the callbacks -- M2
census.method: for each callback of each primary module, compare against the callback at the same index of every OTHER module in the installation that has one. Three counts are kept separately: byte-identical on the first 16 bytes; identical unwind shape (prologue size, unwind-code count, handler flags); and identical unwind shape AND identical function length. The length is kept apart on purpose -- vendors ship different CRT versions and the same helper differs by a byte or two in its tail between them

refutation_probes.question: is each TLS callback of the primary modules byte-identical at its entry, and identical in unwind shape, to the same callback of at least 2 independently built modules of this installation?
refutation_probes.result: PASS -- every callback has independent twins
refutation_probes.would_refute: a callback with no twin: unique opening bytes, a unique prologue or a unique unwind shape would make it worth explaining on its own, and would keep Q-8.2 open

detail.reading: the MSVC CRT emits a two-entry callback array (__dyn_tls_init and its dtor companion) for any module with dynamically initialised thread_local storage. A count of two is therefore evidence of MSVC, not of a check

refutation_probes.question: is 'two TLS callbacks' a distinctive shape, or the norm for any MSVC module in this installation?
refutation_probes.would_refute: only the game executables having the shape, which would make it worth explaining

self_test.what_it_proves: the matcher, the encodings and the delimiter test are live for every declared needle. It does NOT prove the needle table is complete -- a product that renamed itself, or one built without any of these strings, is invisible to a name table by construction

tls_callback_shape_comparison.limits: only the first 16 bytes of each callback are compared, and two functions can agree there and diverge later. This bounds the unknown, it does not close it. Closing it means disassembling the callbacks -- M2
tls_callback_shape_comparison.method: for each callback of each primary module, compare against the callback at the same index of every OTHER module in the installation that has one. Three counts are kept separately: byte-identical on the first 16 bytes; identical unwind shape (prologue size, unwind-code count, handler flags); and identical unwind shape AND identical function length. The length is kept apart on purpose -- vendors ship different CRT versions and the same helper differs by a byte or two in its tail between them

tested_surfaces.what_it_does_not_prove: what the callbacks do. This is the single biggest bounded unknown of both questions
tested_surfaces.what_it_proves: that a callback array exists, how long it is, and which section each callback lands in

tested_surfaces.what_it_does_not_prove: signature validity or signer identity -- this tool reads the directory, it does not verify a chain
tested_surfaces.what_it_proves: Authenticode presence, overlay size, load-config guard flags, DLL characteristics

tested_surfaces.covered: 25 PE modules, full file, ASCII and UTF-16LE
tested_surfaces.what_it_does_not_prove: that a name present is used, or that a name absent is not reached -- an import can be resolved by ordinal or by hash, leaving no string
tested_surfaces.what_it_proves: which API names, middleware names, detection constants and tool names appear as literal bytes, with offset, length and containing section

tested_surfaces.covered: 53 files, 5057001973 bytes, middleware and kernel-routine names only
tested_surfaces.what_it_does_not_prove: anything about a name stored compressed or encrypted, which is the normal state of container payloads
tested_surfaces.what_it_proves: that these product names do not appear as literal bytes anywhere in the installation, container payloads included

untested_surfaces.what_would_close_it: disassembly of the call sites -- M2 work (plan.md section 7)
untested_surfaces.why: this tool does not disassemble. Whether any of the imported functions is CALLED, from where, and whether its result reaches a branch that changes behaviour, is unread

untested_surfaces.what_would_close_it: nothing admissible: D-02 forbids decrypting shipped containers. This stays a bounded unknown by decision, not by omission
untested_surfaces.why: the middleware name pass covered every byte of every file in the inventory, but .ucas/.pak payloads are compressed and the MISERY-Windows.utoc directory index is encrypted (D-02, never decrypted), so a name that is present but compressed would not appear as a literal string

untested_surfaces.what_would_close_it: an external observation of the live process -- module list, handle list, thread list. This is level 1 of section 8 and is itself gated on these answers
untested_surfaces.why: nothing was executed. A protection layer that is downloaded, unpacked or injected at run time leaves no trace in the image on disk

untested_surfaces.what_would_close_it: network observation, which section 8 does not propose
untested_surfaces.why: nothing about a dedicated server, a backend, or EOS-side checks can be read from a client image

untested_surfaces.surface: the Steam client layer outside the installation
untested_surfaces.what_would_close_it: steam-metadata: the appinfo record for the appid. Out of scope for a binary-analysis pass
untested_surfaces.why: Steam's own VAC module lives in the Steam client, not in the game folder, and was not examined. Whether this appid is VAC-enabled is a Steam-side fact

untested_surfaces.surface: the two TLS callbacks of each game executable
untested_surfaces.what_would_close_it: disassembling the two addresses in each image and following what they call -- M2
untested_surfaces.why: their addresses, their section and the bytes at those addresses are recorded, but their instructions are not decoded. A TLS callback runs before the entry point and is the classic anti-debug hook site

what_would_change_the_answer: a kernel driver, a service registration, or a launcher stub appearing in a later build of the installation
a middleware name appearing in a container payload once a legitimate route to read one exists
a call-graph pass (M2) showing a self-check or a blacklist comparison inside the game image
an observation of the live process showing a module that is not on disk
